clean_target_drill.method: Seeded 2 candidate objects (real media bytes on disk), 1 promoted master head, and its durable project event into a disposable PostgreSQL database + disposable media root, via the exact repositories the product uses. Created a backup set, then genuinely destroyed the source (DROP DATABASE, rmtree the media root), then restored into a second, independently disposable, empty database + empty media root.
clean_target_drill.post_restore_verification: verify_restored_backup_set: accepted=true, checked_media_count=2, checked_master_count=1, zero reason_codes. Additionally re-read the restored data through the same repository/query paths the product uses (CandidateObjectRepository.get_exact, a direct master_head_versions row read) and confirmed every field round-tripped, proving the ADR-0089 P0 item 5 bar directly: selected projects and masters remain resolvable, not merely byte-identical on disk.
clean_target_drill.rpo_rto_definition: RPO measured as the gap between the last durable write before backup creation and create_backup_set's own recovery_target timestamp (same-process wall clock). RTO measured as the wall-clock duration from the start of restore_backup_set through the end of verify_restored_backup_set. Both are same-machine, same-process, disposable-container measurements -- not representative of a real network-attached restore's transfer time; see coverage_limitations.

h6_backup_and_restore.scope_note: Golden A/B (M3/M6's own fixture generators) were not invoked directly for this drill: pg_dump/pg_restore operate on the whole database regardless of which tables are populated, so the backup/restore mechanism's own correctness does not depend on which fixture produced the rows. The drill instead seeds a representative cross-section (candidate/master/event) directly through the same repositories M3/M6's own code paths use, and proves resolvability through those same repositories post-restore.

coverage_limitations: No independent (Codex or otherwise) review was run against this exact HEAD; status is a human/self override per status_note above.

The restore drill and all PostgreSQL testing used fresh, empty, single-node local Docker containers; it does not exercise production-scale connection pooling, replica failover, network-attached storage transfer time, or the CI runner's exact resource profile. Measured RPO/RTO reflect a same-machine, same-process, disposable-container round trip, not a real cross-network restore.

pg_dump/pg_restore client/server major-version compatibility is a real, observed operational hazard (see the module docstring in r2/host_hardening/backup.py and the runbook) -- this milestone's own testing used a version-matched client/server pair; a mismatched pair in a real deployment would need the same care documented in docs/r2/runbooks/m7-backup-restore.md.

No automated write-fence: create_backup_set proves (does not assume) that no candidate mutation happened during its own run, but a real production backup still requires the operator to stop the application/worker first, per the runbook's Preconditions section.

The restore drill seeds a representative cross-section of the durable ID chain (candidate/master/event) directly through the product's own repositories, not the full M3/M6 Golden A/B fixture-generation pipeline; see h6_backup_and_restore.scope_note.

H7 telemetry wiring covers only the execution-recovery scheduler; other execution-pipeline seams (submission, promotion) do not yet emit spans. This is a real, disclosed gap, not a claim of complete instrumentation.
Provider qualification (H8) is explicitly out of scope for this file; see provider_qualification_deferred above.
Frontend (pnpm check) and website checks were not run in this session; M7-D touched zero files under frontend/ or website/ (confirmed via git diff --stat against the M7-C head).
